What the data will not support

Pavements are not measurable from OpenStreetMap. In Rotterdam the sidewalk tag appears on 0 of 68,464 roads, and only 30 km of footway is explicitly tagged as pavement against 3,551 km of road. Absence in the map says nothing about absence on the ground.
Traffic calming measures mapping effort, not streets. 17.15% of Rotterdam segments are calmed against 0.62% in Genova — a 27.6× gap from 3,806 mapped features against 73. Both cities report full coverage. Coverage proves observation, not comparability.
Terrain changes the comparison, not just the numbers. Routing on flat distance made Genova look comparable to Rotterdam (reach 0.481 against 0.508). Routing on slope-adjusted walking time over a 30 m elevation model drops Genova to 0.305 and Rotterdam only to 0.462 — the gap between the cities was understated 5.8×, and 12.6× once weighted by residents. Genova is denser but cannot convert that density into access on foot.
Only 3 of 9 indicators survive two cities. Speed limits are tagged on 79.3% of Rotterdam roads and 9.4% of Genova's, so that indicator drops out of any cross-city claim.

Caveats

Population is total residents, not children — GHS-POP carries no age structure. Catchments overlap, so per-school figures must not be summed to a city total.
